content: 1. Individuals who are vulnerable in offline environments are also more susceptible to risks in online settings. Protective factors in offline environments can similarly reduce exposure to online risks. 2. Governments play a critical role in mitigating risks and addressing the needs of children in the digital environment. This can be achieved by implementing policies and regulations that create a safer digital space. 3. Adolescents’ capabilities differ based on their age, maturity, and circumstances. Therefore, actions and policies targeting adolescents in the digital environment must be age-appropriate, tailored to their developmental differences, and consider their varying access to digital technologies, which is influenced by socio-cultural and socio-economic backgrounds, as well as the involvement of parents, guardians, or caregivers. 4. A national child online protection strategy should be developed, ensuring a safe, inclusive, and empowering digital environment. This strategy must integrate with existing policy frameworks related to children’s rights and complement national child protection policies by addressing all risks and potential harms in the digital space. 5. Online risks should be addressed through specific policy actions, including: Standardizing the definition of a child as anyone under 18 years of age in all legal documents to ensure consistent enforcement of protections against online abuse. Collaborating with independent human rights institutions for children to safeguard their online protection through specialized expertise, investigations, monitoring, awareness campaigns, and education. Directly consulting children in the development, implementation, and monitoring of child online protection frameworks or action plans. 6. Legal frameworks should be reviewed to ensure they provide the necessary powers for law enforcement and other relevant actors to protect individuals under 18 from all forms of online harm across all platforms. 7. Any illegal act against a child in the physical world must also be deemed illegal in the online space. 8. Online data protection and privacy rules for children must be adequate and aligned with international standards, laws, and conventions related to children’s rights and cybersecurity. 9. Law enforcement agencies must handle cases of children harming others online in accordance with child rights principles, favoring approaches other than criminal law application. 10. Adequate financial and human resources, as well as training and capacity-building, should be provided to law enforcement to effectively address online risks. 11. International cooperation among law enforcement agencies should be strengthened to enable quicker responses to online-facilitated crimes. 12. Businesses should be obligated to conduct due diligence regarding child rights and safeguard their online users. 13. Monitoring mechanisms should be established to investigate and address violations of children’s rights, improving accountability for ICT companies and other relevant entities. 14. Regulatory agencies should develop standards relevant to children’s rights and ICTs, ensuring the industry adopts a “safety and privacy by design” approach in their products, services, and platforms. 15. The industry must use rigorous mechanisms to detect, block, remove, and report illegal content and abuse involving children. 16. Child-friendly reporting mechanisms should be provided by the industry to allow users to report issues and seek further support. 17. National public awareness campaigns tailored to various groups (e.g., parents, social media users, industry) should be developed to address issues related to the digital environment. 18. Educators and school administrators must be trained to identify and respond to suspected or confirmed cases of online child abuse. 19. A comprehensive digital literacy program should be developed to equip children with the skills to identify threats, understand the implications of their online behavior, and fully benefit from the digital environment. 20. Digital literacy components should be integrated into the national school curriculum, ensuring they are age-appropriate and applicable from an early age. 21. Educational resources outside the school curriculum should emphasize the positive and empowering aspects of the internet while promoting responsible online behavior. 22. Fear-based messaging should be avoided in educational programs. 23. Children, parents, and caregivers should be consulted in the development of online educational programs, tools, and resources. 24. Road traffic injuries are a leading cause of death among adolescents, with younger adolescents being more vulnerable due to their limited physical, cognitive, and social development. Older adolescents may engage in riskier behaviors, such as speeding. 25. Road safety measures, including speed management, improved infrastructure, and enforcement of traffic laws, are essential to protect children and adolescents. 26. Low-speed zones (30 km/hr) should be implemented around schools and areas with high pedestrian activity, along with traffic-calming road designs and enforcement of speed limits using automatic speed cameras. 27. Data collection should be improved to identify high-risk areas and inform effective policies and interventions. 28. Collaboration among institutions and stakeholders across sectors (e.g., education, health, local government, transport, and police) is crucial to enhance road safety for children. 29. Schools and students should be engaged in road safety policy decision-making. 30. Partnerships among communities, schools, and police should be established to manage school crossing patrols and initiatives like “walking buses.” 31. Safe infrastructure, such as sidewalks, safe crossings, and traffic-calming measures, should be prioritized to protect children traveling to and from school. 32. Vehicle safety standards should be improved for child passengers by applying UN minimum safety regulations and promoting consumer awareness of higher safety standards. 33. Laws requiring the use of child restraints in vehicles and helmets for two-wheeled vehicles should be strengthened and enforced. 34. Trauma response measures should be improved to address the needs of children involved in road traffic accidents, including training teachers and school transport drivers in immediate injury stabilization. 35. Urban planning must consider adolescent-specific and gender-responsive aspects, ensuring safe public spaces free from physical hazards (e.g., pollution, waste, traffic) and social risks (e.g., crime, exclusion, bullying). 36. Industrial parks should address youth-specific needs, such as vocational training opportunities, age-adjusted labor conditions, and occupational health and safety measures. 37. Public spaces should be designed and maintained to ensure accessibility and safety for children of all ages.
